title: The Verge’s Duo Review: ‘Apple’s Folding Phone Is a Messy, Expensive Good Time’
content:
Nilay Patel and Allison Johnson (also: 26-minute video review on YouTube):

This means almost every time you open the phone you instinctively rotate it, and while it will work no matter how it’s rotated, it’s better to rotate it counterclockwise so the cameras are on top and the volume buttons are on the top left. Over our week of testing, this started feeling more natural, but it’s exactly the opposite of what you’d initially expect. It’s especially odd in Apple’s bumper case, which has a large notch to expose the Touch ID sensor and camera control, and it looks for all the world like it belongs at the bottom.

You might think this is a little thing, but it’s strange to find yourself slightly unsure of how to hold a smartphone. A nontrivial part of the Duo experience is just reorienting yourself to where the volume buttons are as you flip the thing around. When closed, they’re on top of the phone, but if you rotate the Duo clockwise, they end up on the bottom right, and it’s the top button that turns the volume down because they don’t change orientation with the display. There’s a buried setting in iOS that makes the volume buttons reorient themselves as you turn the Duo around; Apple needs to set it so it works right by default.

Completely agree with them on this — it seems inexplicable that with default settings, while holding the open Duo vertically, if the volume buttons are on the right, you press the up button to lower the volume and down button to raise it.

One other thing to get used to is simply unlocking the phone. Touch ID is integrated into the wake button on the side of the phone. There’s no Face ID at all, and it might take a minute to remember that when you stare at your phone for a beat and wonder why your notifications aren’t unfurling. Ask us how we know. But a week is long enough to get used to Touch ID life again, and it’s mostly painless once you remember you’re supposed to be using it.

Completely disagree with them on this — unless you wear an Apple Watch all day every day.

Re: the cameras, they make this interesting aside:

(It would be cool if you could switch the image preview to the other panel to use it halfway open like a waist-level viewfinder, but you can’t.)

This is a great opportunity for third-party camera apps. Imagine using the Duo in the L-shaped laptop pose, holding it at waist level, looking down — like a Hasselblad 500.

Overall Patel and Johnson are fair and astute, but far more positive about the iPhone Duo than me or Joanna Stern. Don’t get me started on The Verge’s 10-point ratings scale, but they scored the Duo a 7/10, and only gave last month’s iPhone 18 Pro an 8/10. Based on this description of their scale, I’d give the 18 Pro a 10/10 (“best of the best”) and the Duo a 4/10 (“mediocre — has multiple outstanding issues”).

Critique and writing (permalink)

Through my own writing life, nothing has done more to improve my writing than diligent participation in peer-based workshops; that's where a group of writers, all at about the same stage in their artistic development, gather to read one another's work and offer feedback specifically aimed at improving each other's stories.

This is a deceptively simple exercise, and the reasons it works so well are quite counter-intuitive. The most obvious benefit is the way that a workshop encourages you to write at all. When you're at the start of your writing career, you are almost totally reliant upon your own internal self-discipline to keep producing.

Acquiring that self-discipline is infinitely valuable, but it's also incredibly hard. Being part of a group of writers who expect you to regularly turn in new work adds a very useful bit of external motivation that augments your still nascent self-discipline. Knowing you have to turn in a story for the group by Friday can get you in gear when you feel discouraged or blocked.

Before you're getting published regularly (or at all), your critiquing circle might be the only source of validation you get for your work, so the knowledge that you're in for that validation if you get that story in on time is a great motivator. But this is where the counter-intuitive part comes in: as great as it feels to be the center of your peers' attention and to get close feedback on the work you sweated over, that's not the real value you get from a writing workshop, at least not at the start of your career.

Your peers' critiques can help you fix weaknesses in your story, and even teach you a little about how to avoid those weaknesses in future work. You might get feedback that turns an unpublishable story into a published one. But the point of a writing workshop isn't merely to make your stories better – it's to make you better at writing stories.

That's where critiquing other writers' stories comes in. The process of reading and re-reading someone else's imperfect work and devoting real mental energy to figuring out what's not working in it and how to fix it is how you develop the creative instincts that allow you to automatically and unconsciously avoid pitfalls and make breakthroughs in your own work.

Even if none of the feedback you offer is ever incorporated into the story you're critiquing, the act of preparing and delivering that critique is the most reliable fast-track to becoming a better writer yourself. There's something very valuable in the combination of thinking critically, being exposed to other workshop members' ideas about the story under discussion, and working with source material that you can look at with more objectivity because it didn't come out of your own head.

I bring all this up because I've now heard from a few beginning writers who tell me that they're finding LLMs to be good editorial feedback generators. They value the editorial suggestions they get from a chatbot after they finish their work, and use it to help them with a new draft. Without commenting on whether I think LLM feedback is editorially useful (I certainly wouldn't ever ask a chatbot for that kind of feedback), I want to point out that when it comes to improving your writing, getting editorial notes on your work is distinctly inferior to offering criticism of other writers' work.

The reality is that when you're starting out as a writer, the vast majority of work you produce will be artistically unsalvageable. The much-vaunted "million words of crap" you write on the way to becoming a publishable writer are about learning to marry technique to artistic vision and to sharpen both. Getting editorial feedback that helps you shore up the weakest spots in a story that is ultimately never published and constitutes a learning exercise has value, but it has far less value than applying the things you've learned from making and fixing those mistakes to your next story.

With vanishingly few exceptions, a commercially and artistically successful writer isn't someone who writes one great story or novel: a writing career is defined by a body of work, which means that you have to do more than rewrite. You have to write the next thing, and the next thing, and the next.

Having an editor-on-demand of highly variable (and often dubious) quality might help you improve your writing, but it's no substitute for participating in a peer workshop. The idea that an LLM might be able to stand in for a workshop is grounded in the fallacy that the point of a workshop is to have people tell you how to fix your story, rather than analyzing other people's writing in order to develop your own critical skills.

Look: it's a cliche to say "every writer is different," but I really believe that every writer is different, and that's down to the legibility of the writing process to other writers. If you're a painter or sculptor or other visual artist, you've likely spent many hours in a studio with many other practitioners while all of you work from the same life model or still life. If you're a musician, you've almost certainly played music with other musicians. If you're a dancer, you've definitely danced with other dancers.

But writers get precious little exposure to other writers' process. At best we might look at each other's drafts. A musician can listen to every note another musician produces while riffing or composing a new work or interpreting a work. Writers don't get to watch words emerge from each other's fingertips. Being observed that closely while you write would be ghastly and paralyzingly invasive.

I've taught a lot of writers over the years and I've had many discussions with my peers about their writing process, and I'm here to tell you that pretty much every writer finds every other writer's process baffling. We each of us invent an idiosyncratic process for ourselves that will never fully work for anyone else.

So if you value editorial feedback from a chatbot (ideally, a local one running on your computer and not one of the "foundation models" that are torching the planet and elevating the worst people on earth to positions of political, technical and commercial prominence), that's fine, you do you.

But even if that's the case, I still want you to know that whatever you're getting out of the chatbot is fundamentally different, and (I believe) much less useful than participating in a peer workshop.

That's what I wanted to say today, but I predict that an appreciable number of readers are about to email me to ask how these "peer workshops" work. There's a ton of variability in how these are conducted, but the basic shape of them is that in advance of each session, one or more writers submits a finished work to the other writers, who then read through the manuscript at least twice, making notes that include both minor copyedits and broader, thematic notes. They may write a brief editorial response as well, ranging from a paragraph to a couple of pages.

Then the workshop convenes. Each writer briefly expresses their views about the story under consideration, focusing on those thematic and structural notes on what worked and didn't work in the story, with suggestions for improving the latter. You don't need to point out every typo – they're noted on the manuscript. Critiquers don't need to repeat one another. If another workshop member says the thing you were planning to say, you can just say "Ditto what so-and-so said about whatever." If you have nothing to add when your turn comes about, it's fine to pass.

Those are pretty much universal characteristics of a peer workshop. Here are some variations that I am dogmatically committed to, but which other workshoppers might disagree with:

  • Every writer should submit regularly to the workshop. There is a serious risk that attending a workshop can become a substitute for actually writing. It is no kindness to your workshopmates to let them stay in the circle if it leads them to stop writing.

  • The subject of each session must not speak during the critiques, except to answer direct questions that are not related to the writing itself (e.g., "I couldn't figure out what word this was supposed to be – can you clarify?"). The subject can speak after all the other writers have spoken.

  • Each person in the critiquing circle speaks once, in turn, without being interrupted. No cross-talk allowed. It is useful to set a time-limit for critiques.

  • No partial manuscripts. It's not really possible to critique a story unless you have the complete tale. Novels can be workshopped as three chapters and an outline.

  • Stories should be distributed in advance and read in advance. Don't have writers read their work aloud for critique, as this can lead to critiquing the delivery rather than the material.

  • Critique the story, not the writer. It's fine to be offended by something in the story, but not OK to accuse your workshopmates of being bad people for having offended you.

  • Discourage resubmission of revised stories. Workshopping produces sharply diminishing returns. If you really want feedback on a rewrite, approach people individually and ask if they'll read the new draft.

Any group of three or more writers can start a workshop. You'll need to locate writers who are at about the same stage in their artistic and professional lives as you, and find a physical place (or a videoconference service) where you can meet. Library meeting rooms are a favorite, and so is rotating between workshop members' homes. Set a regular schedule – weekly, fortnightly, monthly, possibly quarterly – and stick to it.

title: "No way to prevent this" say users of only language where this regularly happens
content:
In the hours following the release of CVE-2026-89078 for the project Ruby, site reliability workers and systems administrators scrambled to desperately rebuild and patch all their systems to fix a double free in Ruby's Onigmo regular expression parser when parsing fails after an alternation, allowing memory corruption and potential remote code execution in applications that compile attacker-controlled patterns. This is due to the affected components being written in C, the only programming language where these vulnerabilities regularly happen. "This was a terrible tragedy, but sometimes these things just happen and there's nothing anyone can do to stop them," said programmer Miss Ebony Reilly, echoing statements expressed by hundreds of thousands of programmers who use the only language where 90% of the world's memory safety vulnerabilities have occurred in the last 50 years, and whose projects are 20 times more likely to have security vulnerabilities. "It's a shame, but what can we do? There really isn't anything we can do to prevent memory safety vulnerabilities from happening if the programmer doesn't want to write their code in a robust manner." At press time, users of the only programming language in the world where these vulnerabilities regularly happen once or twice per quarter for the last eight years were referring to themselves and their situation as "helpless."

A third suggestion from Luca Bacci on creating a fake agile wrapper that is technically agile but is not useful outside its home apartment was to use the COM static store.

The COM static store doesn’t help us, because the COM static store runs down when the last thread shuts down COM, whereas we want something that runs down when a single apartment shuts down COM.

There is a per-apartment version of the COM static store, but it is part of the Core­Application­View, which is (1) something that only UWP programs have, and (2) exists only for apartments that have a core application view, and those are restricted to single-threaded apartments.

Even if there were a per-apartment static store, putting something into it would require generating a unique name and remembering it for later removal. You could probably use the stringified address of the object, with a fixed GUID prefix as a pseudo-namespace. Since we’re dealing with a dictionary, the insertion and removal operations are going to be O(log n) or O(1), depending on the implementation, but even the constant-time version will have a higher constant than a single index lookup in the Global Interface Table.

title: How I use AI on this blog
content:
Inspired by this LessWrong post, I thought I'd write about how I use AI here. This is less in the interest of disclosure, more to provide a snapshot of what I'm doing right now so that I can revisit it in the future and see how it changes. And hey, maybe it'll be of interest to you, dear readers.

If I were to summarise my working philosophy in fewer than ten words, it would be: AIs identify problems and I fix them myself. With a very specific kind of exception (which I always flag), the text and code on this blog are human-generated. That's not a moral stand, but more a constraint imposed by what this blog is meant to be -- a place for me to learn in public.

Ideation and running experiments

Every post here is based on an idea I had, and work that I've done. For many posts -- for example, the large-scale coding projects like this one -- I'll have multiple chat sessions ongoing while I do the work, normally with either ChatGPT or Claude, or sometimes both. The amount of input they have varies, but because the value of these projects is in what I learn when I'm doing them, letting an AI do my thinking for me would make the whole thing pointless -- so I take steps to stop that from happening.

AIs are, of course, trained to be helpful, and will often explain things in their replies that I would have better learned on my own through experimentation. I'm generally pretty good at spotting when that happens before I've read more than a sentence or two, though, so I can skip reading that part, scroll straight down to the input field, and ask it to operate in more of a rubber duck mode.

With the most complicated projects, where each step has a hard dependency on having got the previous one just right, I do use AIs for code review. Let's say that I've built a model that I intend to extend. I'll test it myself (does the loss go down when training, is it generating plausible-looking results?), but if I want to be really cautious, then I'll run the code past an AI. I'll paste it into a chat session and tell the LLM what it's meant to do, and ask it to check if I've screwed up 1. Again, though, I make it clear that I don't want it to make fixes -- just to point out any bugs.

Writing things up, and the editorial board

As things progress with a project, I keep detailed notes. When I'm done, I write them up without AI assistance, getting the post to a level where it might be a little messy in terms of how things are explained, but all of the important information is in there. I read it through and make sure I'm reasonably happy with it, and then it's time for what I've taken to calling the editorial board.

I paste the draft post into a fresh chat session with an LLM -- right now, this is normally Claude -- and ask for comments. It already has enough information in its memory of earlier conversations to know that what I'm looking for: places where I'm confidently wrong or other technical errors, places where my explanations are missing a step, or where I'm overexplaining things, conclusions that don't really follow from the results of an experiment, and that kind of issue. It tends to spot a few silly grammatical errors and typos at the same time. An important standing instruction is that I do not want it to rewrite anything. Just as with the code, it should tell me where there is a problem, and let me fix it.

We iterate on that for a while until we have something that we're both happy with, and then I feed it to the next LLM -- normally ChatGPT.

ChatGPT has a much more pernickety attitude than Claude does. I often use metaphors, and it will generally want me to replace them with mathematically rigorous prose. This is still very useful, though. Sometimes the metaphors aren't flagged as such well enough -- or even worse, there are times when the terms I've hit on for a metaphor happen to clash with a technical term, making what I've written misleading at best.

I don't always address all of the issues that ChatGPT raises, as otherwise every post would be a mess of hedges and overexplanations and what-have-you, but I like to get to a stage where I'm comfortable that I have a good understanding of specifically why I'm rejecting the remaining points it raises.

One other point where ChatGPT has helped a lot is that it's very diligent about checking supporting materials that I link to. When I was recently about to post an article on running an eval on a model, it followed the link to the training code and spotted a silly bug. It wasn't something that materially changed the eval's outcome, which is probably why I'd not noticed it, but it was something that was important to get right if I wanted later runs of the same evals to be solid. Definitely helpful.

With that done, I run it past a cast of other LLMs. The exact set varies over time; for the last few posts it has been (in this order) DeepSeek, Grok, GLM-5.2 and Kimi K3. I did use Gemini in the past, but over time it became less effective and just started complimenting me on the post and suggesting related topics to chat about, which was kind of pointless. I'll wait until the next release and then try it again.

Because the Claude and ChatGPT passes have generally got rid of anything particularly nasty, this second group of AIs often don't have much to add. However, occasionally they will spot something the others have missed, or have other suggestions, so it's worth spending the five minutes or so it takes to use them. It also helps to keep me up to date with what the other models out there are like. 2

When all of that's done, I run it past Claude one final time, tidy up any remaining issues, then publish it on a private staging site, and read through it carefully myself. The best time for that final readthrough is after dinner, ideally after a glass of wine; the goal is to smooth out the prose, and remove anything overly formal. To make it as close to being fun to read as I can manage.

Once I'm happy, I can promote it to the live site and hit the publish button.

That probably all sounds much more complicated than it actually is. A short post will normally go through all of that in half an hour -- less if I skip the full editorial board, which I sometimes do. The longer ones can take an hour or two, but given that they're normally the result of a week of work, on and off, in percentage terms it's not that much, and it's worth it for the polish.

So, there's no AI-generated text here, but I do lean on AIs to make it the best version I can of what I have to say. How about the code?

AI coding

Again, the goal of the projects I document here is to learn in public. If I'm learning some concept that is expressed in code, then I need to write that code. So that means that anything non-trivial will be something I've written by hand, with AI input limited to code review -- the same rule as I have for the text.

Of course, sometimes there are things I'd like to publish that I wouldn't learn anything by writing. Coding up matplotlib stuff to chart loss curves, or writing a fancy JavaScript visualiser to show what models' parameters are used for would teach me nothing. So for that kind of thing, I just let the AIs get on with it (and even then, for the parameter visualisation, I hacked a first version together in a spreadsheet to check my understanding, and then tested the visualiser against it). I do always mention in the text when a particular bit of code was AI-generated, though.

So, my rule is: if I would learn something by writing the code, I'll write it. If not, I'm happy to delegate to an AI.

But even then, I apply one restriction: if it's for the blog, I'll ask for the code in a chat session, rather than using a more agentic system like Claude Code or Codex. This is to add friction. If you're using an agent, it's easy for a task to grow, and what started as a throwaway idea can come to consume more and more time and cognitive space. Keeping it in the chat interface keeps things minimal -- or at least, that's how it works for me.

Does that mean that I'm against coding agents?

Yes to agents, but not on this blog -- yet

This blog is where I post about experiments I've done and what I've learned. At the moment, what I'm learning is all pretty low-level. How does an LLM work? What factors make it smarter or dumber? It's all pretty hands-on, and involves code that I need to understand.

I do other things apart from writing this blog, of course :-) And for that I'm keen on agentic tools; I have an OpenClaw agent to help me run my life generally, and use Codex and Claude Code for projects where I'm trying to achieve a specific goal, rather than trying to learn something. But by their very nature, those are not projects that will wind up here on the blog right now.

That might change in the future! When I feel that I have a solid, large enough foundation, perhaps I'll be running experiments that I want to write about, where it would make sense for AIs to handle the details, while I focus on the broader strokes.

But that time is not now, so right now, you can be sure that every word 3, and almost every line of code, was written by hand. Even if I do need the AIs to keep me on track and at least borderline coherent.

  1. If you're wondering "why not use Claude Code or Codex", I get into why I avoid them for blog-related work towards the end of this post. ↩

  2. Current thoughts:

    • DeepSeek used to be close to Claude and ChatGPT, but has been left somewhat behind. I have been hearing rumours on X of an upcoming update, though.
    • Grok used to have a propensity to try to turn my posts into clickbait. It would always want to rewrite things, and would suggest titles that were not a million miles away from "Ten things you never knew about RNNs -- number four will shock you!" Recent releases have been much better, though, and I might experiment with moving it further forward in the sequence.
    • GLM-5.2 recently complimented me on my "science fiction" blogpost that mentioned ChatGPT 5.6 Sol. I probed it a bit on that and it said that because the publication date on the post was in 2026, it understood that I was writing near-future SF. From its perspective, the real date was sometime in late 2024. Surprising! I think the last time I saw that kind of behaviour from a model was, well, sometime in 2024...
    • Kimi K3 is really quite impressive. I will be using it more. I particularly like the way it shows a fairly detailed chain of thought -- something it shares with DeepSeek and GLM-5.2, but there seems to be more depth there. It's a pity that Claude and ChatGPT only show summaries in the chat interface, though I understand their reasoning.

    ↩

  3. ChatGPT, being wonderfully true to form, thinks I should clarify here that I'm not including quotes from models here (like the ones here) when I say that. ↩

title: Premium: The Hater's Guide To Blackstone
content:
For whatever reason, Blackstone founder and CEO Stephen A. Schwarzman has a thirty-chapter-long series called “My Personal History” that is, well, exactly what it sounds like — a financial hagiography that frames him as a noble, sensible man with strong values, like when he sent a letter to “distinguished skull and bones alumni” Averell Harriman, whose father Edward Harriman had crashed the stock market in 1901 in his dogged attempt to monopolize the post-bubble railroad industry. Averell himself had co-founded a bank with Fritz Thyssen, who banked the nazis.

Anyway, seven chapters in, Schwarzman makes a bold claim while telling the story of his first job on Wall Street in 1969, where he saw the oncoming collapse of a nearby student fridge rental and life insurance business (no, really):

I knew at once that the business could not last. Students kick refrigerators, throw them around and break them in no time. And a 20-year-old believes he will live forever; he has no interest in life insurance. 

A visit to the company confirmed my suspicions. No one there seemed to know who was sitting in the next room. It looked like a growth company only because the number of students kept rising. Internally, it was out of control. I went back to the office and wrote a report concluding that the company would, in time, go bankrupt. Soon after, it did.

You may not be able to read a financial statement, but you can still recognize madness and folly. When weighing an investment, there are questions one must ask. Does the company have a real reason for being? Are people going to get excited about its products? Are the people running it authentic and focused, or are they merely salespeople trying to persuade you of something that is not real?

Good question, Steve! 

While we’re on the subject, why is it that you invested $275 billion of Blackstone’s roughly $1.4 trillion in assets under management into data center and digital infrastructure investments? While people might get excited about their products, I have it on good authority that the $2.3 billion debt financing deal you did for CoreWeave (back when, per The Information, it only had $16 million in revenue) closed despite everybody having serious misgivings about the financial health, ongoing returns and actual viability of the business.

Based on everything I’ve learned about Blackstone, it appears that the only people you do business with are “salespeople trying to persuade you of something that is not real”! 

Let’s go down the list:

  • Blackstone-owned medical device rental company Apria Healthcare paid, per the Private Equity Stakeholder Project, its owners $210 million in dividends in the same month that it paid a $40.5 million settlement related to its fraudulent billing practices, otherwise known as defrauding the sick and elderly. Great job guys!
  • In 2019, per Housing Is A Human Right, the UN’s special envoy on the Right To Housing and the chair-rapporteur of the UN’s Working Group on human rights sent Schwarzman a seven-page-long letter stating that Blackstone was "significantly contributing” to the financialization of housing, which was “having a grave impact on the enjoyment of the right to adequate housing for millions of people in the world,” with Blackstone-owned Invitation Homes’ jacking up leases, charging tenants for repairs, forcing people out of their homes, and its overall financialization of housing directly discriminating against African Americans, to name only a few of the horrors caused by this company.
    • I go into more detail about this in the piece.
  • In 2018, Blackstone bought Atlanta-based Packers Sanitation Services. Five years later in 2023, PSSI was forced to pay a mere $1.5 million to the Department of Labor for, to quote TIME, “...[employing] more than 100 children—some as young as 13—were employed in hazardous jobs cleaning equipment like skull splitters, brisket saws, and bone cutters in meatpacking plants in eight states over the course of three years.”
  • In March and July 2021, Blackstone would take its payments platform PaySafe and benefits platform Alight public via two separate SPACs with billionaire Bill Foley, with the stocks peaking at $185 and $260 a share respectively. Their stocks are worth $5.51 and $9.16 as of writing this sentence, with effectively anyone who invested during the IPO utterly screwed.

Blackstone is the world’s largest commercial landlord, the world’s largest private equity firm, and the largest investor in data center infrastructure. It has invested in and/or loaned money at least once to OpenAI, Anthropic, CoreWeave, Google TPUs, Firmus, a private equity vehicle to sell Anthropic’s software, Lambda, and innumerable amounts of random AI startups and AI infrastructure companies at a scale that is hard to quantify for reasons I covered in both the Hater’s Guides to Private Equity and Private Credit, which mostly stem from the word “private.”

Nevertheless, even from the outside, Blackstone’s exposure to AI — and the greater software industry — is distressingly large, and thanks to that privacy, it’s very, very hard to tell where the money is coming from, both in the case of where Blackstone gets its funds and what specific vehicle it’s deploying them from. 

Put another way, you can find Blackstone’s fingerprints on almost every big AI deal, yet more often than not have no way of saying what specific fund sunk in the cash. 

Blackstone, as the Ur-Private Equitor, is not one company but a labyrinth of different investment funds, each funded by a combination of corporate pension funds, sovereign wealth funds, horrifyingly, public pension funds, which Bloomberg Intelligence estimates accounts for 32% or so of Blackstone’s overall funding.

Today, I’m going to dig into how credit, insurance and big bets on AI have changed one of the most evil companies in the world.

title: An Ion Storm!, Part 2: The Return to Ground Level
content:
Stevie Case and John Romero early in their courtship.

This article tells part of the story of John Romero.

Note that there is a sexually suggestive image below that may be Not Safe For Work!

In the badlands of what used to be Texas, rumor has it that John Romero has thrown himself out the window of Ion Storm’s penthouse offices. Apparently Romero had finally finished Daikatana, only to have the Y2K bug destroy the gaming rigs of the world mere seconds later, thus rendering the last three years of Romero’s life terribly, terribly moot.

— Computer Gaming World, January 2000 issue

When Stevana “Stevie” Case arrived for her freshman year at the University of Nebraska in 1996, her conception of digital games was limited to the likes of Super Mario Bros. The daughter of a science professor, she had grown up in Kansas in comfortable middle-class surroundings, a precocious overachiever who told her family early on that her goal in life was to become the first female president of the United States. As her first steps toward that position, at age seventeen she had unsuccessfully run for the Kansas state legislature and successfully run for president of her high-school student body, in which capacity she had shaken hands with Bill Clinton. Now, she intended to become a lawyer as her next steppingstone to Clinton’s current office. She was already familiar with the inside of a courtroom, because she and her family had sued her school in federal court for banning Annie on My Mind, a young-adult novel about a lesbian relationship, from its library. They had won the suit, forcing the school to reimburse their costs and, most importantly, return the book to the library shelves. Prim and articulate, Stevie Case gave every sign of being destined for a bright future in the public sphere.

But then, almost as soon as she arrived at university, some of the young men who lived in her dorm complex showed her DOOM and Quake. She was immediately transfixed. Hyper-competitive ever since she had muscled her way onto a boys’ T-ball team when she was barely out of preschool, she adored the deathmatch ethos: “It was really fast, and you felt like you were flying through that world. And then when you added the ability to compete and beat other people, it just felt really addictive. I was all about the rockets and blowing shit up.” She was soon spending far more time playing Quake than studying.

These were the dawning days of what we call e-sports today, when deathmatchers were beginning to organize themselves into teams and leagues and hold tournaments to test their mettle against one another in public. This burgeoning culture of competition was clustered around the nation’s universities, whose fast local-area networks made it possible. Case won her first Quake tournament at her university in January of 1997, playing as the only woman on a team called Impulse 9. Her personal handle was KillCreek, after a Midwestern indie-rock band by the same name. She was a solid enough player, but it was her gender that truly made her stand out; her fame as “the girl who is pretty damn good at Quake” spread quickly online.

Despite his responsibilities as a founder of Ion Storm, man-of-the-people John Romero was still an active participant in the deathmatch community. “Hey, I know a girl that can kick your ass,” said a member of his circle. “No way. Never happen,” he replied.

One thing led to another, and it was arranged for the two of them to meet and do battle that spring, during a road trip to Dallas that Case and some of her friends had already planned. That semi-anonymous city of technology and finance, so often overshadowed by oil-rich Houston, music-rich Austin, and romantic San Antonio, had finally forged a proper identity for itself, among people like Case at any rate, as the wellspring of first-person shooters, home of id, 3D Realms, and now Ion Storm. For a shooter fan in 1997, making a pilgrimage there was akin to a flower-power hippie hitchhiking to San Francisco 30 years earlier. And now Stevie Case was not only going there, but going there to meet the fragger-power movement’s equivalent of Jerry Garcia.

When Romero walked into the room in his full rock-star regalia, she perceived him as a “god”: “And I’m just some person from Kansas. I had no idea if I could beat this guy or not.” As it turned out, she couldn’t, at least not on this occasion. She put up a decent fight, but Romero won fairly easily. Afterward, he posted online that “deathmatch is a man’s game and women will never fully understand it.”

Still, the novelty of a girl who could play Quake decently well was difficult for the community to resist. Encouraged to try again, Case publicly challenged Romero to a rematch, a best-of-three this time, with the loser expected to create an “online shrine” to the winner. Pressured by his own fans to pick up the gauntlet, Romero agreed to her terms. And so, once again, Case made the trek to Dallas — her ambition to become president, and with it her studies, had pretty thoroughly fallen by the wayside by now — to join battle with gaming’s biggest rock star.

She came prepared this time, having learned a bit about Romero’s play style from the previous match, more from talking to others. Her newfound confidence caught him by surprise; she won the first game handily. Romero then buckled down and took the second one, trash-talking ever more volubly and profanely as he did so, with plenty of disparaging references to her gender. The momentum seemed to be with him going into the final match. Case was thrown back on her heels in the early stages of the tiebreaker. But then…

“I’m hearing him say this running sexist commentary,” she remembers, “and it’s like something snapped in my brain. It was just this moment of, ‘Fuck this, this is not happening!’ So, I went on a rampage.” She turned the tide and won the game. As she recalls it, Romero responded ungraciously, by smashing his keyboard to pieces in a fit of pique and storming out of the room. Once he had calmed down, however, he did create the online shrine demanded by the terms of his deal with Case, even if he couldn’t resist making a backhanded excuse for the loss: “Maybe someday I will learn the secret of her master ability, or maybe next time I will, uh, eat some food before playing.”

When Case returned home from university for summer break, she told her confused parents that she was dropping out and moving to Dallas. She rented a truck, filled it with her things, and drove south to her gaming promised land.

She found herself a job there in tech-support to pay the bills, and renewed her connection to Romero through the new Cyberathlete Professional League, an organization that had him on its board of directors and routinely conducted its meetings in Ion Storm’s offices. The same species of awed, slightly clueless mainstream journalists who would soon be trooping through the Ion Storm penthouse in Chase Tower beat a path to the CPL’s door as well, trying to understand and translate what was going on there to their viewers and readers. Case made for a compelling human-interest story, being virtually the only female about the place. She began to appear with some regularity in their reporting. Her role as a mascot was valuable enough that the CPL agreed to pay her a fixed monthly stipend of $1000.

Cases’s prominence undoubtedly helped to lure more women into the scene, although they would always remain a decided minority. John Carmack was recruited to hand out the grand prize at one deathmatch tournament for women only: a signed garter belt. Such a prize encapsulated the queasy mixture of empowerment and objectification that came to characterize the female participants’ experience of this testosterone-soaked realm of endeavor.

Like her peers, Case enjoyed some of the attention that came her way thanks to her gender, but by no means all of it. Her email inbox filled up with messages from men, everything from shy inquiries into her relationship status to meticulously detailed fantasies of sex, rape and sometimes murder. She had never spared that much effort on fashion before, favoring low-maintenance bobbed hair, baggy sweaters, and jeans. But on Halloween in 1997, she went to a deathmatch party dressed as a femme fatale in a tight black dress, and was amazed and gratified by the reaction it provoked, the sense of power it gave her. Around the same time, she found herself cornered in the car of a creepy fellow who had offered her a ride, who now demanded that she show him “it” — meaning her vagina — as payment for the lift. On the spur of the moment, she did as he asked, pulling down her pants to give him a quick peek as he licked his lips in shocked silence. Again, this act seemed to turn the tables on her harasser, to give her power over him.

So, Stevie Case began to radically alter her appearance and demeanor. She had her hair styled, bought a new wardrobe, hit the gym daily, put increasingly revealing and provocative photos up on her personal website, eventually bought herself the most widely discussed breast implants in the history of gaming. “I’ll never regret having a breast augmentation,” she would say to Rolling Stone magazine in 2000. “Did people look at me differently? You’re damn right they did!”

In a sense, Case was of a piece with other unlikely suspects who found some form or other of satisfaction through sexual exhibitionism on the early Web. Whether her moves were the “correct” response to the challenges she faced, whether her newly sexualized persona reflected genuine empowerment or merely internalized misogyny, isn’t a question I can answer for you. I will only venture to say that, if a woman was going to try to turn the male gaze against itself in this way, the deathmatch scene was probably a fairly safe place to do it in comparison to many others, if only because most of its young male participants tended to be more talk than action when it came to matters sexual, not having a surfeit of experience with same in real life. (To wit: the stunned posture of Case’s harasser in the car…) They were well-primed to be cowed by, for example, an all-woman team going under the name of PMS, what with the vagaries of the female body and psyche still being such a mystery to most of them.

Case was well into her transformation in July of 1998, when she became a permanent resident of the Chase Tower penthouse suite, having been hired by Ion Storm as a tester. Shortly thereafter, she began a romantic relationship with the newly divorced John Romero. At a glance, they looked like a rock star and his supermodel girlfriend: he in his leather and chains, she in her leopard pants and high heels. The mainstream press took it as just one more layer to the human-interest story. The gaming press, just about out of patience with Romero eight months after the infamous “bitch” advertisement, was less positively disposed toward his new girlfriend.

Then came the walkout of the heart of the Daikatana team in November. Looking for loyalty in a workplace riven with rumor, innuendo, and guile, Romero promoted Case to level designer, the position she had had her eyes on all along. “I was ecstatic,” she says. “I felt like this brotherhood of designers had accepted me.”

Alas, it didn’t quite turn out that way in practice. Many in the shooter fraternity perceived Case as gaming’s Yoko Ono, an interloper whose talents lay strictly in the direction of distracting her man, stirring up dissension, and raising her own media profile. Their comments could get really, really ugly: “Just another slut that swallowed her way to fifteen minutes of fame”; “Yeah, she’s John Romero’s slut”; “She sucked about 80 dicks to get into games.”

The months that followed Case’s promotion were not easy ones for Ion Storm. On January 14, 1999, The Dallas Observer, a free local newspaper best known for concert reviews and singles ads, published an unusually lengthy piece of investigative journalism. Under the innocuous-sounding headline “Stormy Weather for Popular Computer-Game Company,” journalist Christine Biederman, a future recipient of the Pulitzer Prize, expended 7000 words detailing Ion Storm’s checkered history and what she described as its “toxic mix of prima donnas and personality cults,” sourced largely from an extensive tranche of emails smuggled out of the place by disgruntled current and former employees. It hit the world of gaming like the bombshell it was. I was playing games only occasionally at the time, but I nevertheless vividly remember stumbling upon the exposé for the first time in a copy of the Observer lying on the table in my workplace break room and reading it through in slack-jawed disbelief. The stir it caused came down to its truthiness, the way it confirmed in stark black-and-white newsprint everyone’s worst suspicions. Needless to say, copies of the article were all over the Internet within hours. Although none of the principals are much inclined to thank Biederman for writing it even today, none have refuted her reporting in any serious way either. (I relied on it extensively for the previous article in this duology.)

As if to confirm Biederman’s claims, Romero had to go to Eidos soon after the article dropped to tell them that he would not be able to deliver Daikatana to them that spring, as he had promised to do before most of his development team had walked out the previous autumn. He did his best to mollify the impatient publisher by pointing to his recent hiring of Chris Klie as the project’s new lead designer and Stephen Ash as its latest lead programmer. Both arrived from LucasArts, where they had worked together on the Western-themed shooter Outlaws and the expansion pack to Jedi Knight. Their arrival in Dallas really did bring some much-needed professionalism to the team.

But even when Romero made wise choices for his game, external events conspired to undermine him. On April 20, 1999, came a shock felt round the world, when two alienated teenage shooter fans — deathmatch handles “RebDoomer” and “Vodka” — walked into their high school in Columbine, Colorado, and shot the place up with portable arsenals that were all too real, killing 14 people and injuring another 23 before turning their weapons on themselves. For all his wild-man reputation, Romero had more natural empathy for the parents who were left grieving for their senselessly murdered offspring than did most hardcore players of his games, having brought three children into the world himself with his two wives. He still calls that April 20 “one of the darkest days of my life,” a day which forced him to confront the question of his own culpability in what had transpired. He had never shot a real gun in his life, had never imagined anything like this, had always assumed that the people with whom he deathmatched were just like him, with no interest in turning the bloody hyper-violence they saw on the monitor screen into a tragic lived reality. Now he had learned in a single searing instant that this was not uniformly correct.

From the moment the news programs broadcast footage of police officers carrying DOOM paraphernalia out of the perpetrators’ bedrooms, Columbine transformed the mainstream culture’s perception of id, Ion Storm, and all of their fellow travelers. Since the last brouhaha over violence and sex in videogames, the one initiated by Senator Joseph Lieberman in 1993, had convinced the industry to grudgingly accept a content-rating system, the subject had been treated with more bemusement than real concern even in non-gaming circles. But now, Lieberman was back, more exercised than ever, calling for “a ceasefire in the virtual arms race” with new allies by his side, such as the syndicated columnist Ellen Goodman, who claimed that the military was using DOOM to “desensitize” new recruits to the horrors of combat in advance, and President Bill Clinton, who held up some of the more macabre advertisements for “so-called first-person-shooter videogames” during a press conference. Gaming executives rushed to sanitize and/or postpone their latest hyper-violent releases.

It would all blow over in time, as these things always do; by the following spring, Electronic Arts would dare to belatedly publish Soldier of Fortune, which upped the ante on grisly violence higher than ever through “26 different hit locations on each enemy for pinpoint accuracy and realism!” Nonetheless, for many who had come of age with shooters in the freewheeling 1990s, deathmatch would never feel quite the same again.

The 1999 E3 show took place just a month after Columbine, still very much under its cloud. Ion Storm brought all three of their works in progress. Deus Ex was looking very promising indeed; it was shown off by Warren Spector, pleasant and articulate as ever and, it was now more obvious than ever, very eager to distance himself and his game from the rest of Ion Storm. Tom Hall’s Anachronox looked interesting, if massively under-baked for a game that had been in active development for almost two and a half years. (To be fair, this project had tended to get the short end of all of the sticks at Ion Storm.) But Daikatana… Daikatana was a disaster. For some reason that even Romero didn’t understand, the frame rate of the demo at the show was painfully, unplayably slow. “What the fuck is going on? What the fuck happened?” he could be heard to shout from his company’s booth, his rage and stress palpable. Ion Storm had become a laughingstock yet again.

As Romero has long told the story, the cause of the disaster was Todd Porter, who had ordered some last-minute changes to the build of the demo that was sent to E3, then never bothered to see how it performed. Romero says that, after two years of constant low- or high-intensity conflict with his cofounder, he finally reached his breaking point at this juncture: he went to Eidos just after the show to tell them that “either Todd goes or I go. There’s always some kind of bullshit going on.” This was an odd ultimatum to lay down on the face of it, considering that Eidos did not formally own even a piece of Ion Storm at this point, and thus ought not to have anything to say about its personnel decisions — but then again, nothing about the relationship between the two companies was typical, much to Eidos’s chagrin. Even the Tomb Raider juggernaut wasn’t enough to offset the constant drain on Eidos’s finances that propping up Ion Storm had become; the publisher posted a substantial loss that year.

However it transpired, a deal was engineered over the next few months, in which Eidos would pay Todd Porter and his crony Jerry O’Flaherty a (still undisclosed) sum of cash to leave and would take over the studio completely, forgiving the nearly $30 million they had advanced Ion Storm to date in lieu of any payment to the other two owners. John Romero, Todd Hall, and Warren Spector all promised to stay on as employees at least long enough to finish their respective games. All three were eager to trumpet the acquisition as a turning of a page that would finally let them buckle down and focus on making the best games possible.

Yet even now, the various wars of words in the press continued. Having stolen Romero’s last development team out from under him, Mike Wilson apparently considered his debt of honor duly paid, and now took Romero’s side. He informed Computer Gaming World that Ion Storm was poised at long last to become “the powerhouse it always should have been. Everyone that truly understands the goings-on at that company can tell you that 99 percent of their problems stemmed from Todd Porter and his hand puppet O’Flaherty. It took John and Tom longer than it should have to fix the problem, but the important thing is that it’s fixed, and that the games coming out of that tower look phenomenal. I expect great things from them now.” Not to be outdone, Bob Wright, a corporate lawyer and loyalist of Porter who had helped to set up the studio, riposted that “John [Romero] hates confrontation. John didn’t want to run the business, he just wanted to be a celebrity. [Porter has] a tremendous capacity to rise above impending doom. I’ve never seen anything like it. It’s like trying to drown a cat. He stands on the bodies of the people he’s buried.” (Rather disturbing imagery, that, especially so close on the heels of Columbine.) Gamers lapped it up and waited for the next turn of events in their favorite soap opera.

Like clockwork, Stevie Case now came roaring back into view to add another heaping dollop of sex to all of the delicious backbiting. That fall, she agreed to do a nude pictorial for the Playboy website. The reaction to the photo spread from some gamers was cruel enough to make her begin to question some of her recent life choices. This may not be, she reluctantly concluded, the best way to build a long-lived career for herself as a game designer. “The more I leaned into being beautiful, the more intense the harassment became, and the louder that message of ‘You are worthless!’ came from the community,” she told journalist David Kushner in 2022. John Romero seemed incapable of giving her the sort of support she needed, being still compelled, presumably by his own insecurities, to play the edgelord rock star for his (increasingly disgruntled) fan base. “Just imagine having sex with a super hot model,” he said to one online interviewer who asked about the couple’s love life. “She’s so hot, we have to get back home as fast as possible almost every day! I was going to send some photos, but the attachment was too big.” Case developed bulimia as her self-worth plummeted.

Rolling Stone seemed scarcely less horny than a panting teenage gamer when it did a photo shoot and profile of Stevie Case in 2000. As any real gamer could have told the magazine, the irony of this picture was that nobody played shooters using a joystick anymore. Case had to track down and borrow a suitably phallic-looking example of the peripheral.

In the meanwhile, Ion Storm still had three games to finish — none of which would, a frustrated but unsurprised Eidos was informed, be ready for the Christmas of 1999, thus making that holiday season the studio’s third in a row with no product to sell. Deus Ex at least was looking more impressive than ever, as Warren Spector’s team down in Austin settled in for the sprint to the finish line with camaraderie and purpose. Daikatana and Anachronox, by contrast, were lurching along in an awkward shamble. Daikatana especially exuded the stench of failure and obsolescence. Romero was finding it harder than ever to hold a team together. Chris Klie and Stephen Ash, the veteran hands who were supposed to have been the project’s saviors, both decamped to less chaotic work assignments after less than nine months on the job. Few other established professionals were interested in joining a project and studio that had become a punchline, leaving Romero to rely, this time out of necessity rather than idealism, on yet more inexperienced amateur modders and promoted testers. He insisted to Eidos that the morale and productivity of his team had been tremendously improved by the departure of Porter and O’Flaherty, and he was probably correct as far as it went, but the lack of simple game-making competence among the rank and file was more painfully evident than ever.

Despite it all, Eidos told Romero, who was no longer in any position to argue, that they wanted Daikatana in stores by May of 2000, no matter what it looked and played like at that point. Faced with his first unshiftable deadline, he met it — after a fashion anyway. Daikatana finally shipped. “It was not the game we hoped it might be, but we had run out of time,” says Romero, apparently oblivious to the irony that Eidos had given Ion Storm fully three and a half years and many millions of dollars to make it live up to the hype. Through all the turmoil of the last several years, the basic structure of a battle through time for a magical Japanese sword had remained intact. But the old aspirations to elevate the art of shooter storytelling and make the player cry were comprehensively not achieved. This was a game to make its player cry — and laugh — for completely different reasons.

Daikatana’s use of the two-and-a-half-year-old Quake II engine, coming after id had already dropped Quake III on the world, was the least of its problems. The reviewers who had been waiting for it with knives out were not disappointed; if anything, the game outdid even their high expectations for terribleness. They savaged it with glee. Robert Coffey’s colorful takedown for Computer Gaming World came under the headline of “Yep… It Stinks.”

Daikatana has a story buried in it somewhere, something about a magic time-traveling sword, and some evil guy using it for nefarious ends, and some other stuff, but odds are you won’t follow it. Not that the game fails to devote time to the story. No, the game devotes too much time to the plot, spelling it out in the most tedious cutscenes imaginable. Unbearably long and wordy, the cutscenes are the epitome of the “3D Model Standing Around Bobbing Its Head at Another 3D Model Bobbing Its Head” school of storytelling. An irritating series of swooping camera pans futilely tries to inject life into these stillborn dramas.

Immediately after the opening movie comes the definitive Daikatana moment, a moment you’ll relive hundreds of times throughout the game: you mutter, “What were they thinking?” The game is carved up into four time periods, and the execrable first episode — set in 2455 Japan — brazenly throws down a gauntlet, daring you not to uninstall the game. Drenched from the first second in a godawful puke green, Daikatana wastes no time besetting you with the worst first-level enemies ever, a robotic frog and his buddy robo-mosquito. Almost impossible to see as you tromp through the stereotypical sewers, the poisonous Froginators are as fun as a cold sore and the hideous buzzing of the mosquitoes stays with you even after you’ve left the game. That persistent buzzing is the sound your brain makes as it desperately tries to slither out the back of your skull…

This opening act against mechanical amphibians and insects was inexplicably the hardest of the whole game. “I decided to make the first level super challenging, but players didn’t like that,” says Romero, “something that would surely be revealed in today’s focus-test-driven development.” I’m all for focus groups in general, but I must say that I do wonder why a seasoned designer like him should have needed a focus group to tell him that your on-ramp for your players shouldn’t be a brick wall. It smacks of an old-school, retrograde theory of game design, which says that players need to pay their dues to be deemed worthy of actually having fun. Games can and should be fun from the very start.

Once you got a ways into Daikatana, you met your two companions, the same ones who had been so widely hyped in the early previews. These embarrassing attempts by nerdy white men to capture the personalities of a Japanese woman and a black American man — named “Superfly,” no less! — turned out to be arguably the worst thing of all about this very bad game. They hopped constantly into your line of fire when they weren’t shooting you in the back. From the moment of their arrival on, Daikatana became more of a babysitting simulation than a shooter, as you struggled to devise ways to keep your idiotic companions and yourself alive in the face of the broken artificial intelligence and glitches galore — trying to keep them from getting their heads embedded into the walls and from climbing and falling down the same ladder again and again for eternity. These two dimwits, the death of either of which spelled an instant Game Over, became your true nemeses. Thanks to them, the most frequent adjective applied to Daikatana isn’t any of the more flamboyantly disdainful ones; it’s simply “irritating.” This was the game that it had taken John Romero, the mastermind of DOOM’s most brilliant levels, three and a half years to make?

Word on the street was that it was called John Romero’s Daikatana because nobody else wanted their name associated with this thing.

What does Daikatana have to do with The Muppet Movie? They both start with someone wishing they weren’t stuck in a swamp. (Bah-bum-dum! I’ll be here all week, folks…)

Most agree that the second of Daikatana’s four chapters, which takes place in ancient Greece, comes the closest to being tolerable, with the additions by subtraction of no robot frogs and mosquitoes and companions who mostly take a backseat to the action.

Superfly Johnson (yes, he’s really called that), whose dialog sounds like it was written by that little white-guy rap fan from Office Space. And yes, the graphics really are this bad.

Here we have… you know what? I think we’ve all had enough. Never has a game so made me want to gather all of its makers together in a room and shout at them, “Grow the F up already!”


Setting its many granular infelicities aside, Daikatana just felt old and out of touch, an anachronism from a pre-millennial (pre-Columbine?) version of gaming that had fallen out of the zeitgeist. Oddly for a man so closely identified with the deathmatch, Romero had chosen to focus heavily on the story-driven single-player campaign, leaving the multiplayer mode as an even more broken afterthought; this at a time when online play had become so dominant that id hadn’t even bothered to include a single-player campaign in Quake III. Lingering traces of Romero’s infatuation with Japanese console RPGs showed up not only in its elaborate if incoherent story but in an irritating (there’s that word again!) console-style save system that required you to collect and expend in-game gems for the privilege of being able to step away from your computer for a little while. If there was one thing hardcore shooter fans were not looking for in 2000, it was a game that reminded them of Final Fantasy. Small wonder that, after all the time and all the drama that had gone into making it, Daikatana sold just 41,000 copies in North America.

From Eidos’s perspective, the one bright spot was that, by pushing Daikatana out first, they ensured that they got the worst over with first. Just one month later, they published Deus Ex to reviews that were as positive as those of Daikatana had been negative. Every inch an immersive sim of the old Looking Glass school, a fine heir to Warren Spector’s work on Ultima Underworld and System Shock, Deus Ex alone would eventually be deemed by many gamers to have amply made up for all of the rest of the Ion Storm fiasco. And it was a million-selling hit as well, a feat of which the Looking Glass games that preceded and inspired it had not been able to brag. Romero claims that “Eidos easily earned out its investment in Ion Storm on Deus Ex sales alone.” Although it’s hard for me to see how this statement could be correct when I sit down to do the math for myself, there can be no question that Spector’s game made the whole Ion Storm train wreck look substantially better from a financial point of view than it otherwise would have. (I’ll dig into Deus Ex and its legacy in more depth in my next article.)

Deus Ex’s success was enough to save the team who had created it; Warren Spector and company embarked immediately on a sequel down in Austin. Meanwhile much of the Daikatana team was unceremoniously let go that summer, the rest moved over to the laggardly Anachronox, all too aware that finishing that game would probably mark the end of their tenures inside the Chase Tower — indeed, of the absurdly costly gamers’ penthouse itself. Now plainly under-populated, with large parts of the space abandoned and closed off to save on air-conditioning costs, the penthouse already felt like a ghost town. No more awed reporters trooped through. Even the gaming sites didn’t much care what went on here anymore now that they had had their fun mocking Daikatana. Ion Storm had become an anachronistic artifact of a different era. The bravado and excess of its heyday seemed silly and passé in this post-millennial context.

Hoping against hope, John Romero busied himself for a while drawing up designs for another shooter that might salvage his reputation and restore his rock-star mojo. But in time he got the message that this was not going to happen — not at this studio, at any rate — and buckled down to help his old buddy Tom Hall make his game as good as he could. When it came out in June of 2001, fully a year after Deus Ex, Anachronox proved a rough-cut gem by any objective standard. Still, it wasn’t another Daikatana; while all too clearly less than what it had been intended to be, it was able to coast a surprising distance on Hall’s native gee-whiz enthusiasm and the likability this instilled. Unfortunately, it didn’t sell very well. (Rest assured that I’ll look at Anachronox too in more detail in a future article.)

With this game done, the two remaining Ion Storm founders quietly shut off the lights at the top of Chase Tower and went home. “See you,” said Romero to Hall as they climbed into their cars in the parking garage. “Yeah, see you,” answered Hall.

And so it was all over, but for Warren Spector’s gaggle of survivors in Austin, who had never had all that much to do with their colleagues in Dallas anyway. John Romero’s adventure in Behind the Music-style excess had led to one awful game in Daikatana, one merely bad one in Dominion, one fairly brilliant one in Deus Ex, and one that lay somewhere in between all of the extremes in Anachronox. All things considered, it could have been much, much worse. Thank God for Warren Spector!

Still, the Ion Storm saga as a whole had already been enshrined in gaming lore as a monument to rampant egotism and entitled indolence. Nobody was knocking at the door to hire John Romero now; one of the two hottest names in the business five years ago, he was now all but unemployable. Longing to recapture the fun of the early days at id Software, when it had just been a matter of a few friends in a clubhouse inventing gaming’s future, Romero formed Monkeystone Games with Tom Hall and Stevie Case. They would forgo the big budgets and large teams in favor of small games aimed at handheld devices like the new Pocket PC, games not all that far removed from the ones id had made before John Carmack turned his friends on to the potential of first-person 3D graphics. To emphasize the sense of a new beginning and raise some much-needed cash, Romero sold his mock-Tudor mansion and his Ferrari; he even cut his hair. Instead of auctioning off his trademark flowing locks for a doubtless hefty sum, he sent them to a nonprofit that made hairpieces for cancer-stricken children. Whatever his faults, John Romero was never a man without a heart.

The pivot to mobile showed prescience about where gaming would go in the smartphone era to come, but Monkeystone was just a little bit too early on that scene, and never made that much of an impact. The same can be said of most of what Romero and Hall did after Monkeystone closed up shop in 2004. Neither has been given the chance to helm another big-budget game since Daikatana and Anachronox; in this sense, their years of excess at Ion Storm continue to haunt them.

For her part, Stevie Case was secretly relieved when the Ion Storm rat race ended, taking with it her fifteen minutes of fame as, to quote Rolling Stone, “a real-life Lara Croft,” on the arm of gaming’s biggest rock star. The end of that era certainly improved her mental health. But it wasn’t enough to save her relationship with Romero in the longer term. Although he was nine years her senior, she felt herself to be growing up in ways that he could not or would not. “He was like a perpetual fifteen-year-old boy,” she says. “That’s ultimately why I wanted to leave him. ‘I’m not fifteen anymore. I want an adult life. I want to have dinner parties and adult friends.’ And he had no interest in that.” The couple split permanently in 2003.

Case never did become president of the United States, but she did go on to a very successful career as a Silicon Valley executive. Today she is the chief revenue officer of Vanta, a digital-security firm worth $4 billion as of its latest valuation. She no longer plays shooters or any other games with any frequency, but says that she will always be a gamer in spirit.

An older and wiser and once more lavishly coiffured John Romero in 2022.

In 2023, John Romero published a memoir called DOOM Guy: Life in First Person. The name is a disarmingly accurate assessment of his current place in gaming culture; he is, quite literally, still “the DOOM guy,” both to gamers of his own generation and those who came later. Unlike his old partner in crime John Carmack, who managed to remain at the forefront of gaming technology for many years after the turn of the millennium, Romero is doomed (ha!) to be remembered for just one decade of his life, bookended by the soaring triumphs that were Wolfenstein 3D and DOOM and the disastrous crash landing that was Daikatana. The table of contents of his book doesn’t lie: 22 out of its 27 chapters are devoted to the years before the closure of Ion Storm Dallas ended his tenure as an A-list game developer, leaving him to summarize the last quarter-century of false starts and nostalgia-fueled celebrity in an anticlimactic whirlwind.

To be honest, I didn’t expect much from his memoir when I picked it up, having always found his rock-star posture be the apotheosis of the grating bro-gamer man-child; I half expected every sentence to begin or end with the word “dude,” as most of his email communications did back in the day. Imagine my surprise, then, to meet a more or less thoughtful and reflective man in its pages, one who fesses up with surprising readiness to many of his mistakes, at Ion Storm especially: “As you read, you will likely note moments where I should have made a different decision or seen the writing on the wall, and you will not be wrong. I own the train wreck that was Ion Storm. If nothing else, writing this book has been a transformative process. It has allowed me to see patterns that have followed and defined me, patterns I may not otherwise have seen.” The book thus makes it clear that Stevie Case was wrong in her assessment of her boyfriend, at least in the long term: this is a guy who can and has grown up. Having lived through the maelstrom of Ion Storm and all that came before and after, John Romero has by all indications come out to a place of acceptance and gratitude, aging far more gracefully than many of his peers. “When I was a kid,” he tells us, “all I wanted to do was wake up and make games every day for the rest of my life. How lucky am I that this has happened?” The rebel has become an elder statesman, always ready with a pat of encouragement and a word of advice for young would-be game developers who aren’t so different from the kid he used to be.

In retrospect, I shouldn’t have been so surprised that John Romero, like all of us, can contain multitudes. There were always hints of it to be found, such as in his expressed desire to make a computer game with a story that could make you cry, or the revelation that, in between the bouts of herculean lovemaking that he loved to describe to his slathering fans, he used to read books — yes, actual books — to Stevie Case in bed at night. Quite some years ago now, near the beginning of this history project of mine, Mark Pelczarski, an Apple II magazine columnist and founder of an important early software maker called Penguin, shared this anecdote with me.

John Romero tracked me down and e-mailed me sometime in the mid-90’s, with a subject line that was simply “YOU!” He wrote this e-mail about how he learned programming back in the early 80’s using [Penguin’s] Graphics Magician and reading my articles, and that’s how he got his start. Actually, I had no idea who John was at the time, but he signed it “John Romero, id Software”, and “id” rang a bell. I thought it was the company that published DOOM, so I looked it up, found I was right, then was startled to find John’s connection to that [game] and his other work. Cool.

Actually, that led to one of my coolest teaching moments. I was teaching freshman/sophomore C++ courses for CS majors, and I mentioned this e-mail from this Romero guy in one of my classes. Turns out I had a student, Chris Avila (now in the software industry himself) who was one of those who held John up to rock-star status. So Chris e-mails John, asking if he really knew me, and John writes him this glowing e-mail about how I was one of his heroes when he was first learning programming, etc., etc. (Chris showed it to me, and it really WAS nice.) So Chris shows up to me next class basically with his jaw hanging to the floor in disbelief, saying something like, “John Romero is my idol, and then I find out my CS teacher is HIS idol….” (his choice of words, probably not John’s), and standing there bug-eyed just trying to grok it all. Priceless.

Shortly after the events Pelczarski has just described for us, Romero held a reunion for many of his game-development heroes from the 1980s up there at the top of the Chase Tower. Most of them, Mark Pelczarski included, were long since out of the industry, and could only gawk in astonishment at the spectacle of what it had become.

The important point here, of course, is that Romero didn’t have to hold this reunion, and yet he did. So, rock on, John Romero… rock on. I suspect that you have always been more generous than not at heart — more generous perhaps than I have given you credit for — even as I know that you have always genuinely loved games.
